c.v: A personal injury case is a claim that someone else’s carelessness hurt you and that the law requires them, usually through their insurer, to pay for it. Most people searching this phrase are not sure yet whether what happened to them is a case. This page is written to answer that first, then to tell you what you can recover, how long you have, what a lawyer costs, and where to go on this site for the specific kind of injury you have.

ATLAW is a personal injury law firm in Dearborn, founded by Dewnya Bazzi. In 13 years the firm has handled more than 10,000 cases and recovered more than $100 million for clients in Wayne, Oakland, Macomb, and Washtenaw counties. Consultations are free and available in English, Arabic, and Spanish, and we take injury cases on contingency: no fee unless we recover money for you.

sections.heading: Do you have a personal injury case? The four things Michigan law requires

c.v: Every personal injury claim in Michigan, whether it is a car crash, a fall, a dog bite, or a surgical error, has to prove the same four elements. If you can answer yes to all four, you likely have a case.

items.v: The other party owed you a legal duty of care. Every driver owes it to every other road user. A store owes it to customers. A doctor owes it to patients. A landlord owes it to tenants. This element is rarely disputed.

They failed to meet that duty. A driver ran a red light. A store left a spill on the floor for an hour. A surgeon operated on the wrong site. In Michigan, the standard is what a reasonably careful person (or a reasonably competent professional) would have done in the same situation.

The breach caused your injury. This is where insurers fight hardest. They will argue your back pain came from a pre-existing condition, or that you would have been hurt anyway. Medical records dated close to the incident are the answer.
You suffered a real loss: medical bills, lost wages, pain, a changed life. An incident with no injury is not a case, however careless the other party was.

c.v: Michigan adds one more hurdle in car accident cases. Because the state has no-fault insurance, your own insurer pays your medical bills and lost wages regardless of fault, and you can only sue the at-fault driver for pain and suffering if your injury is a “serious impairment of body function” under MCL 500.3135. The car accident page explains that threshold in detail. It does not apply to falls, dog bites, medical malpractice, or any case that did not involve a motor vehicle.

sections.heading: What if you were partly at fault?

c.v: (MCL 600.2959). Your recovery is reduced by your percentage of fault. If you are found 20% responsible for a fall because you were looking at your phone, you recover 80% of your damages. If you are found

at fault, you cannot recover non-economic damages at all, though you can still recover economic damages reduced by your share. Insurers assign fault to injured people as a negotiating tactic; a lawyer’s first job is often to push that percentage down with evidence.

sections.heading: How long you have: Michigan personal injury deadlines

c.v: The statute of limitations is the date after which a court will not hear your case no matter how strong it is. Michigan’s general rule is three years, but several common situations have shorter deadlines that catch people by surprise.

rows.v: Most injury claims (car crash, fall, dog bite, product)
2 years from the malpractice, or 6 months from when you discovered it, with a 6-year outer limit; a Notice of Intent must be sent 182 days before filing
3 years from the death (with a limited extension for the estate’s representative)
Written notice to your insurer within 1 year; unpaid benefits recoverable only 1 year back from filing
Claims against a city, county, or the state (a government vehicle, a defective road or sidewalk, a public building)
Written notice within 120 days, served on the correct agency and officer; the notice must state the injury, the defect, and the witnesses
Generally at least 1 year after the 18th birthday

A fall on a city sidewalk, a crash with a DDOT bus or a county plow, an injury in a public school: 120 days, in writing, to the right office, or the claim is gone.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a personal injury lawsuit in Michigan?

answer.v: Three years from the date of injury for most claims (MCL 600.5805). Medical malpractice is two years. Claims involving a government body require written notice within 120 days. No-fault benefits after a crash require notice to your insurer within one year. Minors generally have until a year after turning 18.

faqs.question: How much is my personal injury case worth?

answer.v: It depends on the severity and permanence of the injury, your economic losses (medical bills, lost wages, future care), how clearly fault can be proven, and the available insurance. Nobody can give you a number before reviewing the medical records. We will give you an honest range once we have.

faqs.question: What does a Michigan personal injury lawyer cost?

answer.v: ATLAW works on contingency: no fee unless we recover money for you, and the fee is a percentage of the recovery set in writing before we begin. Michigan caps contingency fees in injury cases at one-third of the net recovery. The consultation is free.

faqs.question: Can I still recover if I was partly at fault?

answer.v: Yes, as long as you were not more than 50% at fault. Your recovery is reduced by your percentage of fault. Above 50%, you lose the right to non-economic damages.

faqs.question: Is Michigan a no-fault state for all injuries?

answer.v: No. No-fault applies only to motor vehicle accidents. Falls, dog bites, medical malpractice, and other injuries follow ordinary negligence rules: the at-fault party (through their insurer) pays.

faqs.question: Does Michigan cap pain and suffering damages?

answer.v: Only in medical malpractice cases, where the cap was $569,000 (or $1,016,000 for the most severe injuries) in 2024 and is adjusted each year. There is no cap in car accident, premises, dog bite, product, or wrongful death cases.

faqs.question: Will my case go to trial?

answer.v: Most do not. The large majority of Michigan injury claims settle with the insurer before trial, often after a lawsuit is filed but before a trial date. A firm has to be willing to try the case for the insurer to pay fair value, but trial itself is the exception.

faqs.question: How long does a personal injury case take?

answer.v: Simple claims with clear fault and completed treatment can settle in a few months. Most take one to two years, because the value of the case cannot be known until your doctors know how well you will recover. Cases that go to trial take two to three years.

faqs.question: What if the person who hurt me has no insurance?

answer.v: In a car crash, your own uninsured motorist coverage (if you bought it) and your no-fault PIP benefits apply. In other cases, we look for every potentially responsible party: a property owner’s insurer, an employer, a manufacturer, a bar that served a drunk driver. An uninsured individual with no assets is, realistically, difficult to collect from, and we will tell you if that is the situation.

faqs.question: Should I accept the insurance company’s first offer?

answer.v: Not before a lawyer has reviewed it. First offers come early for a reason: the insurer wants to settle before the full extent of the injury is known. Once you sign the release, the claim is closed permanently, even if you need surgery six months later.
